Pet turf for Reunion's tight villa yards

Pet turf in Reunion runs $10–$18 per square foot installed, typically $12–$16, as of September 2026, a step up from a plain lawn because of the drainage base and odor-control infill. A lot of Reunion's dog owners are working with a fenced strip beside a zero-lot-line villa rather than a wide-open backyard, which changes the layout more than the price.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say you have a narrow side yard

Say you have a 12-by-30-foot side yard beside a Reunion villa, about 360 sq ft, that two dogs use several times a day. At $10–$18 a foot with zeolite infill, that comes to roughly $3,600 to $6,480, with most jobs this size landing near $12–$16 a foot, or about $4,320 to $5,760. Because the strip runs against a wing wall on one side, access is limited to hand carts rather than a skid steer, which is typical for this lot type and is already built into that range rather than added as an extra. Skipping the weed barrier and grading the base to drain toward a corner catch point keeps standing puddles from forming after a Florida afternoon storm, which matters more here than on a wide-open lawn since the whole strip drains through one exit point instead of spreading out.

Small footprints, real drainage needs

Zero-lot-line villas and townhomes are common inside Reunion's gates, which means a dog's daily yard is often a narrow side strip or a small fenced rear pad rather than a full lot. A tight footprint doesn't lower the drainage requirement: urine and rinse water still need somewhere to go, so we build the same washed, open-graded crushed rock base under a 200 sq ft dog run that we'd use under a 2,000 sq ft lawn, just shaped to fit the space.

What the pet turf price range covers

Installed pet turf runs ten to eighteen dollars a square foot, typically twelve to sixteen, running higher than a plain lawn because the backing, base depth, and infill are all upgraded specifically for a Reunion dog yard rather than shared with a standard residential build. That premium isn't padding: a deeper washed-rock layer, a fully permeable backing, and zeolite or coated sand all cost more to buy and install than their lawn-grade equivalents. A homeowner comparing a lawn quote against a pet turf quote for the same square footage should expect the difference to show up specifically in those three line items, not in the visible turf blade itself.

Why we skip the weed barrier under dog turf

A weed barrier that works fine under a family lawn becomes a problem under pet turf, because it traps urine at the fabric layer instead of letting it pass through to the base, which is where the odor starts to build. On a small Reunion side yard where a dog is out several times a day, that trade-off shows up faster than it would on a bigger lot with lighter traffic, so we leave the barrier out and rely on the compacted rock base and zeolite or coated infill to keep the smell down instead.

How fast the base under a dog run has to drain

A dog run needs more base depth than a plain lawn, typically three to four inches of washed, open-graded crushed rock or crushed concrete instead of two to three, because liquid volume from daily rinsing and repeated urination is higher than rainfall alone on a Reunion property. That deeper layer, combined with a backing built to pass over thirty inches of water an hour, has to clear a full hose rinse in well under a minute, not just eventually. A base that takes longer than that to visibly clear is too shallow or too tightly compacted for what a dog yard actually puts through it day to day.

Paw safety on a hot Reunion afternoon

Full sun pushes turf surface temperature to 120 to 150°F, occasionally higher, which is uncomfortable for bare human feet and can be worse for a dog's paw pads, especially on a run with no shade at all during peak afternoon hours. A hose rinse before playtime drops that surface temperature 30 to 50 degrees within minutes, which is the fastest correction available on a Reunion run that gets full sun most of the day. Scheduling outdoor time before mid-afternoon in summer, or adding at least one shaded corner to the layout, matters as much as any product choice for keeping a dog comfortable on hot days.

Why seams and edges get extra attention on a dog run

Seams and edges take more stress on a Reunion pet yard than almost anywhere else turf goes down, since a bored or anxious dog will work at a loose corner the way it never would on a family lawn nobody digs at. Seam tape and adhesive go on with the same care as any residential job, but the edge anchoring, nails set every few inches or a bender-board border, gets checked twice before the crew moves on to infill. A perimeter that would pass inspection on a lawn sometimes needs a tighter nail spacing specifically because of what a determined dog will test within the first few weeks.

Checking a dog run's edges after a storm

After heavy rain or wind, a Reunion dog run's perimeter is worth checking specifically, more so than a family lawn's, since a dog will find and worsen a loose edge within days where a lawn with no traffic on it might sit undisturbed for weeks. A lifted corner or a seam that's started to gap gets re-anchored quickly rather than left for the next scheduled maintenance visit, since a determined digger can turn a small gap into a much larger one in a single afternoon.

The CDD's own dog park versus a private yard

Reunion's community development districts maintain shared amenities that include a dog park among the pools and fitness facilities available across the resort reunioneastcdd.com. That shared space handles off-leash exercise, but it's not a substitute for a private, fenced pet yard at the house itself, particularly for a rental home where a dog needs somewhere to go out quickly between showings or check-ins rather than a walk to a common-area park.

Questions people ask

Do I need association approval for a small dog run in Reunion?

Usually yes. The resort property owners association reviews yard changes regardless of size, though a small fenced run tucked behind a side wall tends to move through review faster than a full front-yard project.

What infill keeps odor down best in a small, high-traffic yard?

Zeolite or a coated antimicrobial sand both outperform plain silica for odor in a small space that gets heavy daily use; see the pet turf page for how those options compare on price.
